newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Sellers wait on price dip.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Sellers wait on price dip.

text.p: Demand for Middle East Gulf refined oil products could be on the rise in the coming week if lower prices entice reluctant Indian and Chinese buyers back to the market, Gulf oil traders said on Thursday.
The imminent resumption of Iraqi oil exports and higher U.S. heating oil inventories have pushed Gulf product prices to their lowest level since end-November, tracking weaker crude prices.
The first tanker to export Iraqi crude in six years is expected to begin loading at the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan on Friday, the Anatolian news agency reported.
"Weaker prices provide a decent buying opportunity...India and China have delayed their purchases waiting for weaker prices. Now they have got them," said a trader in the Gulf.
India Oil Corp (IOC) has kept it tender imports to a minimum over the last two quarters because of budgetary constraints, according to market sources.

Sellers are now pinning their hopes on IOC coming heavily back into the market for the country's first quarter agricultural fuel needs and to rebuild stock levels which were drawn heavily down as tender imports were capped, traders said.

Though the sale of between 500,000 and 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi oil under the U.N. "oil-for-food" deal is not expected to lead to serious price falls, the volumes could limit any sustained upward price movement, traders said.
Gas oil was assessed at $29.80 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, falling eight percent since the United Nations on December 9 approved the go-ahead for Iraqi oil exports.
Jet kerosene was assessed at $30.40, down from $31.30 on December 5 and adrift from the December high of $33.55.

Gulf product premiums have remained firm and steady despite weaker outright prices caused by weaker crude, with gas oil talked at a 65-70 cents premium to independent price quotes and kerosene at a 60-65 cents premium.

Many Gulf traders had not expected to see any Iraqi crude on the market until January at the earliest because of a history of delays since the "oil-for-deal" between Iraq and the United Nations was agreed in May.
"It's quicker than I originally thought but we're still not going to see substantial (Iraqi) volumes until early next year," another Gulf trader said.

Crude producers, particularly from Kuwait, United Arab Emirates and Iran, are seen as the most vulnerable of the Gulf states to losing market share when Iraqi crude exports step up, particularly from its Mina al-Bakr terminal.
Premiums for Gulf crudes for December and January delivery have been largely resilient to the prospect of Iraqi barrels.
